64	### ⚠️ Settings (#9b): do NOT ship "Auto-log worn looks" as written
65	
66	The plan specifies *"when on, opening a look after 18:00 local logs it."* **Rejected — opening a look is
67	not wearing it.** `wear_logs` is the foundation of cost-per-wear, streaks, most-worn, gathering-dust and
68	gap analysis, i.e. of everything Pro sells. Logging views as wears inflates all of it permanently, with
69	no way afterwards to tell a fabricated wear from a real one — poisoning the paid feature to save one tap.
70	`MONETISATION.md` §1: *"they pay for it in month three, once the data is theirs."*
71	
72	**Build an evening confirmation instead** (agreed with the user 2026-08-05): if you opened a look today
73	and logged nothing, ask once — *"Did you wear <look> today?"* — **Yes / No**. Yes writes the same row the
74	button writes; No writes nothing and it does not ask again that day. Triggers when the app is next opened
75	after ~18:00 local, so it needs no web-push and is buildable now.
76	
77	Two details that decide whether it helps or hurts: **Yes and No must be equally easy** (a lone "Yes" with
78	a dismiss ✕ gets tapped to clear it, and the data inflates anyway), and it asks only about looks actually
79	opened, most recent first — dwell time is not tracked, so "most recent" is the honest simple choice.
80	
81	It is **bigger than a toggle**, so it wants its own small plan. Settings then ships **rain guard as its
82	only live toggle** — which is that plan's own stated rule: *"rendering a switch that schedules nothing is
83	the lie this plan is trying to avoid."*

## 1. Thumbnail `maxPx` → **480**, one derivative

The plan's number is right, and now there's a reason behind it. On a 390px iPhone viewport:

One surface sets the ceiling — the tallest masonry cell at 3× — and it lands on 480 almost exactly. Everything else is far under. Because the images are `object-contain`, a tall coat is height-constrained (160→480) and wide shoes are width-constrained (125→375), so **480 as max-dimension** is the correct form of the cap, not a width.

Don't add a second smaller derivative for the diary and the goes-with row. It doubles upload CPU and storage to save a few kB on surfaces that are already small, and it adds a third path to `displayPath` that every reader has to reason about.

It's ~271 kB × item sitting at rest: a 100-item closet is ~27 MB of storage and ~0 MB of transfer.

So: keeping it costs almost nothing on the axis that matters, and it's the only re-taggable source if you ever change the tagging schema or the cutout pipeline. And your shoe shows the specific failure that follows from it: the dark panel behind the swoosh is the *same value as the backdrop*, so the model reads it as background and eats a hole clean through the interior. That's black-on-black separation failing, not edge quality.

Ranked by value per unit of effort:

**1. Contrast guidance at capture — free, biggest lever.** No matting model separates a black panel from a black backdrop. The viewfinder already says "on a flat surface"; saying *"on a surface that contrasts with the piece"* costs one string. A capture-time check (sample the border colour, compare to the subject's dominant colour, warn before spending the WASM run) is a small step beyond that.

**2. `model: "large"` → `isnet` full-precision.** One config line. Better interior coherence and edges than fp16; costs a larger one-time model download, which we already cache. This is the cheapest code-only quality bump and the first thing I'd measure.

**3. Stop feeding the model a compressed JPEG.** `processImage` compresses to 0.5 MB/1280px *first*, then segments that. Compression artefacts hurt matting for the same reason `encode.ts` holds the cutout at 0.85 for the tagger — and here we've already degraded the input before the model ever sees it. Segmenting the original `file` and compressing after is a small reorder.

**4. Fill interior holes in the alpha mask.** `output.format: "image/x-alpha8"` returns the raw mask, and a flood-fill from the image borders identifies any transparent region *not* connected to the edge — by definition interior. Fixes your shoe exactly. ⚠️ But it has a real trade-off I won't paper over: a genuine see-through gap — inside a tote handle, a belt buckle, between straps — is *also* interior and not border-connected, so blanket filling would wrongly solidify those. It needs a size threshold tuned against your actual closet, which means measuring, not assuming.

**5. `device: "gpu"` (WebGPU).** Mainly makes option 2 affordable rather than improving quality itself. Needs a capability check and a CPU fallback; iOS Safari support is the open question.

**6. A touch-up brush on the confirm screen.** The honest endgame — Decision 3 already says "AI is ~90% right; the user fixes the rest," and that screen exists for precisely this. But it's real UI that nobody has designed, so it wants a design pass first, not a patch.

My recommendation: **2 and 3 together as one measurable experiment**, re-run against a handful of your real problem items (that shoe included), before touching mask post-processing. > **Not a TDD plan.** Research and open decisions. A plan written from this before the decisions in

**`@imgly/background-removal` is AGPL-3.0, and it is on the critical path of every capture.**

Its own README, verbatim:

> *"The software is free for use under the AGPL License. Please contact support@img.ly for questions
> about other licensing options."*

That is textbook dual licensing: AGPL as the free tier, a commercial licence for everyone else. The
library is downloaded and executed **in the user's browser**, which is conveying it, and AGPL's
copyleft reaches the work it is combined with. Fitcheck is a closed-source product with a planned
€5 paid tier (`MONETISATION.md`).

**This is the same class of problem as Open-Meteo** — a free-tier dependency that is not licensed for
the commercial product being built, sitting on a path every user walks. `docs/STATE.md` already calls
Open-Meteo *"the only item that can stop a launch."* There are now two.

### The escape route is unusually clean

`ThirdPartyLicenses.json` in the installed package lists everything IMG.LY builds on:

| dependency | type | licence |
|---|---|---|
| `onnxruntime-web` | code | **MIT** |
| **ISNET** (`github.com/xuebinqin/DIS`) | **model** | **MIT** |
| `ndarray`, `zod`, `lodash-es` | code | MIT |

**Every ingredient is MIT. Only IMG.LY's wrapper is AGPL.** So the same model, at the same quality,
can run on `onnxruntime-web` directly with no AGPL anywhere — the dependency is replaceable without
changing the segmentation at all.

⚠️ **I am not a lawyer, and this is a legal call, not an engineering one.** What is established here
is factual: the licence text, the dual-licence offer, and that the substrate is MIT. Whether AGPL
actually reaches Fitcheck's bundle is the decision — and it has exactly three answers: buy IMG.LY's
commercial licence, replace the wrapper, or accept the risk deliberately and in writing.

---

## 2. What is actually wrong with the cutouts today

### 2a. We pass no configuration at all

`lib/images/process.ts` calls `removeBackground(original)` with no second argument. The library's
schema (`dist/src/schema.d.ts`) shows what we are therefore defaulting into:

| option | default we get | also available |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | `"medium"` → **`isnet_fp16`** (half precision) | `"large"` → `isnet` (fp32), `"small"` → `isnet_quint8` |
| `device` | **`"cpu"`** | `"gpu"` (WebGPU) |
| `output.format` | `image/png` | `image/x-alpha8` — **the raw mask** |
| `rescale`, `proxyToWorker` | defaults | — |

Three levers we have never touched, on the feature the whole product depends on.

### 2b. The reported failure is black-on-black, not weak edges

The shoe has a dark panel behind the swoosh, photographed against a dark backdrop. ISNet cannot
separate them, so it labels interior pixels as background and punches a hole through the silhouette.

⚠️ **This matters for choosing a fix.** A bigger model narrows this case; it does not eliminate it.
No matting model reliably separates a black object from a black background — that is an information
problem in the photograph, not a capacity problem in the network. **The cheapest real fix is at
capture time, not inference time.**

### 2c. We segment an image we have already degraded

```ts
const original = await imageCompression(file, compressionOptions());  // 1280px, 0.5MB, JPEG
const raw = await removeBackground(original);                          // ← the COMPRESSED blob
```

We hand the model a re-compressed JPEG. `lib/images/encode.ts` already documents why this is bad,
for the tagger: *"heavy compression introduces artefacts that hurt model accuracy."* The same is true
of matting, and here we do it before the model ever sees the picture. Segmenting `file` and
compressing afterwards costs memory and time, and costs nothing in money.

### 2d. We throw the mask away

The library hands back a composited PNG. With `output.format: "image/x-alpha8"` we would get the
alpha mask itself, which is what every post-processing technique needs. Today we cannot inspect,
threshold, feather or repair anything, because by the time we see the result the decision is baked in.

---

## 3. ⚠️ The user's half of the problem, which is larger than the model's

Reading the capture flow end to end, the model is not the weakest link.

### 3a. Nothing tells the user what makes a good photo

`components/capture/viewfinder.tsx` shows framing corners and *"Tap to capture an item"*. The only
guidance is one line below it: *"Snap each piece on a flat surface."* **Nothing mentions contrast** —
the single variable that decides whether §2b happens. A user photographing black jeans on a dark sofa
is set up to fail and never told.

### 3b. The confirm screen shows the damage and offers no way to act on it

`ConfirmForm` renders the cutout large, on `.surface-stage`. If the cutout has a hole, **this is where
the user sees it** — and the screen has exactly one action: **Save**. There is no retake, no reject,
no touch-up. The only escape is to navigate away.

Two consequences:

1. **The user's only options are to accept a damaged image or lose the capture.** Most will accept it,
   and the closet quietly fills with broken cutouts that surface later on the flat-lay and the grid.
2. **Backing out strands the upload.** Both blobs are already in Storage before any row exists — the
   orphan class fixed on `feat/image-weight` (PR #46). Two of the four found locally were 40 seconds
   apart, which reads exactly like *capture → see a bad cutout → back out → retry → back out.*
   **The abandoned-capture bug and the cutout-quality bug are the same user, twice.**

⚠️ And a subtlety worth keeping: `.surface-stage` is a **dark** radial gradient, so a hole that has
punched through to transparency renders **dark on dark at review time** and is easy to miss — then
becomes obvious later on a different surface. The review screen is the one place that should make a
hole loud, and its styling does the opposite.

### 3c. "No cutout" is already a supported state, and nobody uses it

`lib/storage/signed.ts`:

```ts
export function displayPath(item: ImageRow, size = "full") {
  if (size === "thumb" && item.thumb_url) return item.thumb_url;
  return item.cutout_url ?? item.image_url;   // ← falls back to the ORIGINAL PHOTO
}
```

A row with `cutout_url: null` renders the original photograph, everywhere, correctly. The reader
already handles it; the backfill already skips such rows; RLS and paths are unchanged. So **"keep the
photo instead of a broken cutout" needs no schema change and no migration** — only a button that
passes `cutoutPath: null` to `confirmItem`. That is the single cheapest quality win available, and it
is a product decision, not an engineering one.

---

## 4. The options, honestly costed

| # | Option | Quality | Cost / risk | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | **Contrast guidance at capture** (copy, then optionally a border-vs-subject check) | Prevents the worst case entirely | One string; the check is small | — |
| B | **Reject / retake / "keep the photo"** on the confirm screen | Stops bad cutouts entering the closet | Needs design; also closes the orphan path | — |
| C | **`model: "large"` (isnet fp32)** | Modest, real | One line; bigger one-time model download | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| D | **Segment the original, not the compressed JPEG** | Modest, real | Reorder two lines; more memory/time | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| E | **`device: "gpu"` (WebGPU)** | None directly — buys the headroom for C | Capability check + CPU fallback | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| F | **Take the mask (`x-alpha8`) and repair it** — flood-fill interior holes | Fixes §2b directly | ⚠️ See the trap below | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| G | **Own the pipeline on `onnxruntime-web`**, ISNet weights | Same as today, plus everything F needs | ~150 lines we maintain | **MIT — clears §1** |
| H | **BiRefNet (MIT), lite ONNX ~214 MB, 1024×1024** | Best available client-side | ⚠️ See the onboarding trap | **MIT** |
| I | **Server-side or third-party API** (remove.bg, Photoroom, Supabase transforms) | High | Per-image cost forever | — |

### ⚠️ The trap in F, stated before anyone implements it

"Fill any transparent region not connected to the image border" fixes the shoe. It also **fills
legitimate holes**: the gap inside a tote handle, a belt buckle, the space between a strap and a
shoulder, the negative space in an open cardigan. Those are interior and not border-connected too.
It needs a size threshold tuned against the **real closet**, and it must be measured, not assumed.

### ⚠️ The trap in H, and it is a product trap not a technical one

`done/2026-07-16-onboarding-five-capture.md` — **the first five items are captured during onboarding,
before the user has ever seen the magic moment.** A 214 MB model download at that moment is an
activation catastrophe. CLAUDE.md's Decision 2 already accepts "a few-MB first-load model download";
214 MB is two orders of magnitude past that.

**If BiRefNet is ever wanted, it cannot be the onboarding model.** The shape that works is
tiered: ship the small model for the first captures, and offer the heavy one later — as an opt-in
"re-cut this item in high quality" on item detail, downloaded on demand, for the pieces that matter.
That also happens to be a natural **Pro** surface.

---

## 5. What the future makes more expensive

Cutout quality gets *more* load-bearing, not less:

- **Share cards (`@vercel/og`, Phase 2).** The cutout leaves the app and becomes marketing. A hole in
  a shoe is a private annoyance today and a public one then.
- **Women's wardrobe** (`scoping/2026-07-24-womens-wardrobe-scoping.md`). One-piece garments, thin
  straps and sheer fabric are the hardest matting cases that exist. The current model will be worse
  there than it is on menswear, and that fork is where the complaints will arrive.
- **pgvector / CLIP (Phase 4).** Visual similarity is computed from the image. Holes corrupt
  embeddings silently — the failure mode is bad recommendations nobody can trace to a cutout.
- **The 50-piece free closet cap.** Every wasted capture spends one of fifty. A broken cutout the user
  cannot reject costs them 2% of their free allowance.

---

## 6. Recommendation

**Two tracks, because §1 is a decision and §2–3 are work.**

### Track 1 — decide the licence (blocking, not engineering)

Answer §1 before spending anything on C/D/E/F, all of which deepen the investment in an AGPL
dependency. Three options: buy IMG.LY's commercial licence, do **G** (own the pipeline on
`onnxruntime-web`, all-MIT), or accept the risk deliberately and record it.

**My recommendation: G.** It costs ~150 lines, removes a launch blocker, and is a prerequisite for
F anyway — the mask access, the input resolution and the execution provider all come with it. It
turns a legal problem and a quality problem into one piece of work.

### Track 2 — ship the user-side fixes now, they are licence-independent

**A and B, in that order**, and neither touches the model:

1. **A** — say "on a contrasting surface" in the viewfinder. One string, prevents the reported failure.
2. **B** — give the confirm screen a way out: *Retake* and *Keep the photo instead* (the latter is
   free, per §3c). This stops bad cutouts entering the closet, and closes the abandoned-upload path
   that PR #46 currently has to sweep up afterwards.

Then, once Track 1 lands: **D** (segment the original) → **C/E** (bigger model, GPU where available)
→ measure → only then consider **F**, with the threshold tuned on the real closet.

**H stays out of scope** until someone wants a Pro "re-cut in high quality" surface, and it must never
be the onboarding model.

---

## 7. Open decisions — for the user, not the implementer

1. ⚠️ **The AGPL question. Buy, replace, or accept?** This is the one that blocks a paid launch, and
   it is the same shape as the Open-Meteo decision still sitting open.
2. **Does the confirm screen get a Retake / "Keep the photo" control?** It is new UI on a designed
   screen — `docs/STATE.md`'s Profile lesson says do not invent UI, so this wants a design pass, not
   a patch. But the screen is currently a dead end, which is its own design bug.
3. **Is a "re-cut this item" action wanted at all** — free, or the Pro surface H would suit?
4. **How much first-load download is acceptable during onboarding?** Decision 2 says "a few MB". That
   number decides which models are ever on the table.

## 8. What was checked, so it is not re-derived

- `@imgly/background-removal@1.7.0`, `LICENSE.md` = AGPL-3.0; README offers commercial licensing.
- `ThirdPartyLicenses.json`: `onnxruntime-web` MIT, **ISNET model MIT** (`xuebinqin/DIS`), rest MIT.
- `ConfigSchema`: `model` defaults to `"medium"` → `isnet_fp16`; `device` defaults to `"cpu"`;
  `output.format` accepts `image/x-alpha8`.
- `lib/images/process.ts` passes **no config**, and segments the **compressed** blob.
- `displayPath` already falls back to `image_url` when `cutout_url` is null.
- `ConfirmForm` has exactly one action (Save) — no retake, no reject, no touch-up.
- BiRefNet is MIT; `BiRefNet_lite` ONNX ≈ 214 MB at 1024×1024.
- ⚠️ **Not measured:** the actual quality delta of C, D or E on the real closet. Nothing in §4 above
  claims a measured improvement, and it should not be quoted as if it did.

I need to correct something I told you an hour ago, because it changes the decision.

**I said the escape route was "unusually clean — everything under it is MIT, including the ISNet weights."** I took that from IMG.LY's `ThirdPartyLicenses.json`. Verifying it against the source, that manifest is not reliable:

| source | licence claimed for the *same* ISNet weights |
|---|---|
| IMG.LY's `ThirdPartyLicenses.json` | MIT |
| the actual DIS repo (`xuebinqin/DIS`) | **Apache-2.0** — "our code and evaluation metric use Apache License 2.0" |
| `onnx-community/ISNet-ONNX` on HuggingFace | **AGPL-3.0** |

And the more important part IMG.LY's manifest doesn't mention at all: the pretrained weights were **trained on DIS5K**, which ships a separate `DIS5K-Dataset-Terms-of-Use.pdf`. Academic segmentation datasets routinely restrict commercial use, and the repo licence covers the *code*, not the data the weights were learned from.

Three sources, three licences, plus an unread dataset term. That's worse than a clearly restrictive licence, because you can't plan around ambiguity.

## So: is there a free model?

Free *libraries*, yes — `onnxruntime-web` (MIT), Transformers.js (Apache-2.0). Those are genuinely unencumbered. **The scarce thing is weights with clean provenance.**

| model | licence | commercial | fit for flat-lay garments |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISNet** (what we run) | contested — see above | unclear | good, it's what we use |
| **RMBG-1.4 / 2.0** (Bria) | explicitly non-commercial | ❌ needs a Bria licence | good — but ruled out |
| **BiRefNet** | MIT repo, authors permit commercial | likely ✓, same DIS5K question on weights | best quality; 214 MB lite |
| **ormbg** | Apache-2.0, **deliberately trained on openly-licensed data** to dodge exactly this | ✓ cleanest provenance found | ⚠️ **optimised for humans**, wrong domain |
| **U²-Net** | Apache-2.0 | ✓ code; DUTS-TR data is research-only | older, weaker |

`ormbg` is the only one built specifically to have clean provenance — and it's the one whose *domain is wrong*, since it's tuned for people, not garments on a surface.

## The honest conclusion

There is no option here whose weight provenance is unambiguously clean for a commercial product. **That's precisely why IMG.LY, Bria, Photoroom and remove.bg all sell licences** — the market exists because the free path is legally murky, not because the models are hard to run.

Which leaves three real choices, and this one is genuinely a lawyer's call, not mine:

1. **Buy IMG.LY's commercial licence.** Certain, and it *preserves Decision 4* — it's a flat SDK licence, not per-image, so the on-device zero-marginal-cost economics survive intact. Cost unknown; worth an email to find out.
